subject: Chemistry
title: Willow Bark: Nature's Aspirin
description: A micro-lesson that makes Willow Bark: Nature's Aspirin usable.

hook.text: For 3,500 years, people chewed willow bark to relieve pain. The active ingredient became the world's most used drug.

buildup.text: Ancient Egyptians, Greeks, and Native Americans all used willow bark. Hippocrates prescribed it for fever in 400 BC.

discovery.text: In 1828, chemists extracted salicin from the bark. The body converts salicin into salicylic acid, which reduces inflammation.

twist.text: Salicylic acid destroys the stomach lining. Felix Hoffmann at Bayer modified it into acetylsalicylic acid—gentler but effective.

climax.text: Bayer named it Aspirin in 1899. Over 100 billion tablets are consumed yearly. It also prevents heart attacks and strokes.

punchline.text: Tree bark to tablet. A 3,500-year-old remedy became modern medicine.

quiz.question: Why was salicylic acid modified to create aspirin?
options: Salicylic acid damaged the stomach lining, so Bayer made a gentler version
Salicylic acid was too expensive to extract from willow bark
The natural compound lost potency when stored as a pill

details.summary: Willow bark contains salicin, which the body converts to salicylic acid, a pain reliever and anti-inflammatory used for thousands of years. Bayer chemist Felix Hoffmann acetylated salicylic acid in 1897 to create aspirin, reducing stomach irritation while preserving the therapeutic effect.
details.whyItMatters: Aspirin remains the world's most widely used drug, taken by over 100 million people daily. Its anti-platelet properties make it essential for preventing heart attacks and strokes in at-risk patients.
takeaways: Salicin from willow bark is converted to salicylic acid in the body
Acetylation produced aspirin with fewer gastrointestinal side effects
Aspirin irreversibly inhibits cyclooxygenase enzymes that produce prostaglandins

faq.question: How does aspirin prevent heart attacks?
faq.answer: Aspirin irreversibly acetylates cyclooxygenase-1 in platelets, preventing them from producing thromboxane A2, which is needed for platelet aggregation and clot formation..

faq.question: Why did ancient civilizations use willow bark for pain relief?
faq.answer: Sumerian, Egyptian, and Greek texts record willow bark prescriptions dating back over 3,500 years. Hippocrates recommended it for fevers and pain. People discovered its effects empirically long before understanding the chemistry, passing the knowledge through generations of traditional medicine.
